new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls regularly on the penultimate syllable; Kami has no lexical or grammatical tone and no vowel-length contrast. Corroborated by Velten 1900: 2 ('C. Wortton. Derselbe liegt im Allgemeinen auf der ersten Stammsilbe, also meist auf der vorletzten Silbe des Wortes.' = stress generally on the first stem syllable, hence mostly the penult).
new_statements.exceptions: Petzell & Aunio state none. Velten 1900 hedges ('im Allgemeinen.. meist'), framing the rule as first-stem-syllable stress that usually coincides with the penult, without listing exceptions.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement; no discussion of phrase-level stress. Yes/no questions are marked by intonation only (pitch rise toward the end of the last word, fall on the often-lengthened final syllable), sec. 6.7.1.
new_statements.identity_note: Both sources describe Kami G36 (kami1256, ISO kcu) of the Morogoro region, Tanzania; Velten 1900 calls it 'Kikami' (speakers 'Wakami', land 'Ukami') from data collected in Dar es Salaam with speakers from chief Kingo's Morogoro residence. Not to be confused with Kami of Nigeria or other homonyms.

sources.note: Sec. 2.3 'Tone and syllable structure': 'Kami is a language with regular penultimate stress and no tonal contrast, either lexical or grammatical.' Sec. 2.1: no vowel length contrast. Sec. 9: lack of tones unusual for Bantu but shared with Luguru and Kagulu. Sec. 6.7.1: yes/no questions marked by intonation only (pitch rise toward end of last word, drop on last syllable, often lengthened).
